subtitle: Watt-hours a day inside the data center. Each group keeps its own boundary and its own ruler.

groups.label: One person's day: text prompts and video delivery
Another boundary: all products, AI training, and offices

reading: {label}: about {display} a day inside the data center, {share} percent of a household's {house} Wh. {evidence}

rows.label: Average weekly ChatGPT user
rows.equation: Prompts a day x Wh per prompt
rows.detail: A median prompt times a mean count over days of non-use, so a floor. At the 0.34 Wh average-class figure the same count gives 1.25 Wh. The high end uses a count of 8, which is unsourced.

rows.label: YouTube, 88 minutes on a phone
rows.equation: Minutes / 60 x GB per hour x Wh per GB served
rows.detail: 0.66 Wh on measured delivery, 0.251 Wh at the DESNZ follow-up's intensity, and 80.7 Wh at a top-down average that spreads all data center energy over all bytes. The allocation is unsettled, so read this as a range.

rows.label: Instagram, 100 minutes
rows.equation: Minutes / 60 x GB per hour x Wh per GB served
rows.detail: Delivery only: ranking and recommendation compute are unmeasured. 0.111 Wh at the DESNZ follow-up's intensity; the high end is capped at Meta's whole day.

rows.label: Meta, per daily active person
rows.detail: A fleet average that includes WhatsApp-only people, AI training, ads, and offices. It does not bound a heavy Instagram user from above and does not sit on the chat row's boundary, so it is printed and never ratioed.

foot.text: This comparison does not decide a proposal. It says nothing about a site, a stream, a rate class, or Treaty-reserved rights.
